clusters.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things
clusters.neutral_headline: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things

items.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things
items.standfirst: Watching fights wasn't as good as practical experience, but it got the mice halfway there.
items.content: Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 There's something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it's the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watch other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn't watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature. The team assigned male mice randomly to three different groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training involving three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle it out from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them. The ninth day was "fight night," when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents' excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously.Read full article Comments

clusters.neutral_headline: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way

items.title: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way
items.standfirst: "We also have a responsibility to not go too fast and cut too many corners."
items.content: NASA recently announced a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon. The moves were designed to give the agency's lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit. These changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. To understand the implications for the spacecraft, Ars spoke with Kirk Shireman, Human Spaceflight Exploration and Orion program manager at Lockheed.Read full article Comments

clusters.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
clusters.neutral_headline: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage

items.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
items.standfirst: When everything goes down, don’t assume it’s a cyberattack.
items.content: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US. Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence. Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.Read full article Comments

clusters.neutral_headline: Ukraine blew up Putin’s bridge using relay drones to bypass Starlink limits

items.title: Ukraine blew up Putin’s bridge using relay drones to bypass Starlink limits
items.standfirst: Ukraine's strike used homegrown tech while adapting battlefield lessons from its adversary.
items.content: A Ukrainian barrage of missiles and drones collapsed a crucial segment of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Strait Bridge—and Ukraine’s military pulled off the strike deep within Russian-occupied territory without relying on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications to guide the missiles in. On the nights of November 15 and November 16, coordinated waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles caused enough damage to collapse one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch bridge’s roadway for automobile traffic, according to an Institute for the Study of War update. Russian sources claimed several hundred Ukrainian drones first overwhelmed Russian air defenses to pave the way for remote-controlled missile strikes focused on the bridge, with the latter prominently including Ukraine’s homegrown Flamingo cruise missile. The Ukrainian operation adapted a Russian battlefield innovation by using drones equipped with mesh radios to create an airborne communications network, according to the Financial Times. Each networked drone acts as a relay node to extend the communication link between human operators and remotely piloted missiles and strike drones. Russia began using the technique to support long-range drone and missile strikes on Ukrainian cities.Read full article Comments

items.standfirst: Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues.
items.content: A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote. All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee's 13 Democrats were absent. "We're going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs," Cruz said at today's hearing. Nominees are vetted in committees first, and then require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January.Read full article Comments

items.title: Trump abandons his FDA nominee, and Senate scraps vote on his NSF pick
items.standfirst: "This time requires leadership and fortitude," Senator Bill Cassidy said.
items.content: In the span of less than 24 hours, two Trump administration nominees have suffered sudden blows—Trump's pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration and his pick to lead the National Science Foundation. Late Tuesday evening, Axios reported that the White House had abruptly withdrawn its controversial nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA. Overton, a top conservative domestic policy aide in the White House, has drawn criticism and skepticism from Republicans and Democrats alike over her stances on vaccines, abortion, vapes, and birth control. Overton opposes abortion—though perhaps not strongly enough for some Republicans—and supported Trump and Kennedy's decried anti-vaccine policies and statements, vexing Democrats. In her confirmation hearing in September, Overton consistently stonewalled senators on every topic, refusing to directly answer even softball questions from friendly Republicans, leaving lawmakers on both sides of the aisle openly frustrated. The questions she dodged included those on how she would handle the FDA's current safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, which extensive data has established is extremely safe. She also wouldn't say whether she agreed with Trump when he falsely claimed the measles vaccine is "quite lethal" or that children are given vaccine doses the "size of a soda bottle." Overton repeatedly refused to answer whether Trump could ever be wrong.Read full article Comments

clusters.neutral_headline: Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security

items.title: Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security
items.standfirst: Hardened defaults align with DoD standards, but there may be growing pains.
items.content: Microsoft's Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core. Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency's (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG). STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: "The secure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened." The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance.Read full article Comments

clusters.neutral_headline: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details

items.title: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details
items.standfirst: "They are pretty confident that it's going to last a long, long, long time..."
items.content: In the one light-day that humanity's most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again. Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter's moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a "commemorative phonograph record," in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space. About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson. While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs' overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago.Read full article Comments

items.title: Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories
items.standfirst: With MyMems, Wright says he wants to "turn the simulation inward."
items.content: The computer gaming world hasn't heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright's subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA. Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players' memories. MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright's previous projects by "turn[ing] the simulation inward," as Wright's Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning. The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world. “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?" Wright says by way of example in the release. "If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?"Read full article Comments

items.title: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says
items.standfirst: "ULA is a valued partner, and we look forward to Vulcan's return to flight."
items.content: United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that the failure of its Vulcan rocket during a launch on Sunday was caused by inadequate fuel supply. "ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday," the company said in a statement. "While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines." The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket's failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle's main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin.Read full article Comments

clusters.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
clusters.neutral_headline: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review

items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
items.standfirst: Jason and Lucia's crime-heavy love story fuels a wonder of digital urban simulation.
items.content: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers.Read full article Comments

items.title: It shouldn’t be this easy to pedal 25 mph: Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo
items.standfirst: This commuter bike will have you blazing through streets without any range anxiety.
items.content: I’ve had only one experience of pedaling an e-bike after it ran out of juice, but it was enough to make checking the battery display an anxiety-driven habit: “Can I afford to use the highest assist level up this hill? Should I switch to eco mode to preserve power and make sure I have enough to get home with the bike lights on?” These aren’t fun questions to have rattling around in your head while riding home in the dark. But those intrusive thoughts never crossed my mind while I was testing Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo. I didn't experience range anxiety, even while blowing through city streets at 25-plus mph (40.2 kph). The bike has so much juice (840 watt-hours) and power (810 watts of peak power and 105 newton-meters of torque) from Specialized's 3.1 motor system that I could ride as far and as fast as I wanted without worrying about having enough battery to get back home.Read full article Comments

clusters.title: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
clusters.neutral_headline: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status

items.title: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
items.standfirst: Measles became endemic in the US months ago—and it's only accelerating.
items.content: International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings. After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it "shameful" and a "national embarrassment." News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases, more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases. There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week. But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What's happening now is a runaway epidemic.Read full article Comments

clusters.title: Waymo has stopped its robotaxis from driving on the freeway—here’s why
clusters.neutral_headline: Waymo has stopped its robotaxis from driving on the freeway—here’s why

items.title: Waymo has stopped its robotaxis from driving on the freeway—here’s why
items.standfirst: Robotaxis already had to be recalled in May after they entered highway construction zones.
items.content: Waymo is currently restricting its fleet of robotaxis to surface streets after getting into hot water with California over its cars' driving behavior on highways. Specifically, the software tends to drive into construction zones at speed. As first reported by the San Francisco Business Times, this behavior actually drew the ire of California’s DMV earlier this month, which ordered Waymo to stop driving on Californian highways immediately and until it can convince the DMV that its cars no longer “pose an imminent hazard to public safety.” This is not Waymo’s first run-in with this problem. In Arizona, Waymo robotaxis did not recognize ramp closure signs on six occasions in Phoenix in April and entered construction zones. A month later in California, seven Waymo robotaxis entered lanes with active construction. In June, Waymo recalled the almost 3,800 robotaxis capable of highway driving. That problem led Waymo to stick to surface streets only in California after the May incidents until late July, when the robotaxis resumed highway operations. In early July, Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that it began updating the robotaxi software to a version that “improve[s] the recognition of freeway construction zones, more appropriately prioritize[s] construction zones over other freeway hazards, and reduce[s] speed when the AV detects that it may be in a construction zone.”Read full article Comments

items.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
items.standfirst: Word, Excel, and PowerPoint now live inside Copilot; always-on agents are next.
items.content: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work." The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.Read full article Comments
